The product · v1 workflow

A custom model, trained call by call

An AI signal is a custom model trained on a customer's own call data to detect outcomes specific to their business: appointment booked, sale converted, frustration expressed.

v1 asked you to build one by hand: review calls one at a time, mark true or false, 20 true and 20 false per round, repeat.

It was a training tool and a discovery tool. It had only been designed to be the first.

The symptom

The absorbed cost

Sold as
Self-service. Train your own signals on your own call data.
Who could
Power users with a detailed mental model of how the workflow behaved. A few got there by trial and error. Not many.
What they wanted
For Invoca to do it for them. And Invoca did. For some accounts the analytics team ran training end to end, fully white-glove.
The bandaid fix
8 hrs of analytics services bundled with every new AI Gold customer.

The 8 hours is what the problem looked like after they'd already contained it.

Research

Four SMEs who were the users

Four interviews with Invoca analytics services team members. They ran this workflow dozens to hundreds of times, on behalf of customers.

The reframe

The bookends problem

Two failures at opposite ends. The middle worked.

Front door missing
Discovery
No guided entry. Nothing told you what made a good AI signal use case, or what didn't.
Works
Training
Manual true/false review. Meticulous and slow, but it did what it promised.
Back door duct-taped
Validation
No live accuracy check. Real performance swung 5–10% from the training prediction.
Current-state journey map · the shape it came from
Purple = manual Invoca work · Green = in product
The proof
13
rounds one customer trained a single signal, with no acceptable accuracy.
4
rounds to 90–95% accuracy once an analyst scoped the signal properly.

Same technology. Different aim.

The system

Four stages, each closing a named failure

01
Topic Explorer
Closes the missing front door
02
Signal Blueprint
Closes bad scoping
03
LLM-as-a-Judge
Closes the labor cost of training
04
Automated Validation
Closes the duct-taped back door
Stage 01

Surfaces topics automatically from the customer’s own call data, with call snippets as evidence. Split into anticipated vertical use cases and unknown unknowns.

Stage 02

Structured guidance for defining what the signal should find, including flagging use cases AI is weak at. Moves the analytics team’s pre-round-zero process into the product.

Stage 03

A second LLM evaluates calls alongside the custom model. Where they agree, no human input. Where they disagree, the user decides.

Stage 04

Accuracy testing against live call data, replacing the team’s manual spreadsheet spot-checks. Feedback names the limitation when AI is the wrong tool.

Stage 1 · Closing the front door

Show me what's already there

Topics surface automatically from the customer's own call data. Each one carries call snippets as evidence, so you can hear why it surfaced before deciding it's worth a signal.

Split into two lists: anticipated use cases for the customer's vertical, and the unknown unknowns the data turned up.

Entry stops being a blank field and a guess.

Stage 2 · Closing bad scoping

The scoping work, moved into the product

Structured guidance for defining what the signal should find, and what it shouldn't, before round zero locks the definition in.

It also flags use cases AI is weak at up front, rather than after thirteen rounds of finding out.

The analytics team's pre-round-zero process, productized.

Stage 3 · The hardest problem

The human is the tiebreaker

Manual training stays as an option. The new path: a second LLM evaluates calls alongside the custom model.

Where they agree, no human input. Where they disagree, the user decides.

Still in the loop, but only at the decision points that actually require judgment.

Stage 4 · Validation and failure states

Designed for the bad news too

Healthy accuracy
Low accuracy
Critically low accuracy

A product that only tells you the good news isn't building trust.

Outcome

Alignment, and a framing that outlived it

Stakeholders aligned

The four-stage approach was agreed across product, analytics services, and engineering.

The prototype carried it

The Figma Make prototype told the story across multiple stakeholder presentations and earned buy-in for the build phase.

The vocabulary stuck

Analytics services and PMs kept using the bookends framing as a shared lens when scoping signal work for new customers.

The concept was greenlit for build.

Reflection

What I'd do differently

01
Research the validation step with external customers

Internal SMEs are real users, but their expertise masks the problems a first-timer would hit.

02
Keep iterating on the judge and the feedback

The LLM-as-a-Judge interface and the validation feedback system were both still in active iteration. Those are the moments where design either builds trust or erodes it.
